chapter_theme: The eight wives are crowned and the land flourishes under Civakan's single umbrella; then the dancer Anangamalai, whom the usurper once seized, comes to the king with a letter that recalls her devotion, and he receives her, enjoys her dance and takes her to bed.

cast.role: daughter of the Vidyadhara king, defeated by Civakan at the vina
the dancer who loves Civakan, once seized by the usurper; named அநங்க மாலை in 2584
the women who bring sandal, garlands and incense to the couple
the dead usurper, recalled in Anangamalai's letter as the cruel spearman (2587)

2575.reading: The eight women with swollen breasts like lotus buds and honey-dripping garlands reach the rank of crowned queens, and the world bows to them.
2575.nuance: The verse does not name the eight; they are read as the wives Civakan has won in the earlier ilampakams, the last being Ilakkanai.
2575.event: Civakan's eight wives attain the crowned rank and are honoured by all.

2576.reading: Women with soft hair and bud-opening garlands fall at the small feet of the Vidyadhara's daughter.
2576.nuance: Neither the bowing women nor the Vidyadhara's daughter is named. She is taken to be Gandharvadattai, whom the poem has called a Vidyadhara's daughter, set first among the wives; the bowers may be the other wives or her maids.
2576.event: The women of the household bow at the feet of the Vidyadhara's daughter.

2577.reading: Civakan settles on the wives an unfailing income of five and a half crore, with a thousand a day, so that bathing, sandal and cooking are provided for.
2577.nuance: The sum and the line about daily provision (ஆயிர நாடொறு) are hard to fix: the verse may count a yearly revenue, or an endowment paid daily. Only the fact of a settled provision is certain.
2577.event: Civakan assigns the women a fixed endowment for their daily needs.

2578.reading: The forests where elephants once ran in rut now ring with deer-eyed women drinking, and the scorched lands the white chariot crossed are flooded with milk-rice.
2578.nuance: The verse says only that wild and dry lands turned to plenty and pleasure under the king; the cause is left to the surrounding verses on his rule.

2579.reading: With rain abundant the earth-woman brims past her bounds, and ghee-rich food lies in lakes everywhere.
2579.nuance: The last line is closed with என்பவே, 'they say': the poet gives the plenty as report, not as sight.

2580.reading: Under his single white umbrella the cool shade of his grace reaches the sea, so that the lands of effortless enjoyment, the golden land and the serpents' world are ashamed and withdraw.
2580.nuance: போக பூமி is the Jain cosmos's land of enjoyment without labour. The verse uses it as a measure for praise; it does not teach cosmology here.

claims.claim: one king's shelter over the whole earth outdoes the lands of effortless enjoyment

2581.reading: Fish-eyed women and their husbands eat, grow old and travel without hindrance, so the earth is as full as in the first age.
2581.nuance: பண்டை யூழி, 'the ancient age', is the poet's name for a golden age; the verse does not say which.

2582.reading: Lords of battle lands and prosperous lands cannot get audience and find no room for the rare ornaments they carry as tribute; the kings of single lands bow, and the able lord's victory stands high.
2582.nuance: The names in line 1 (செருநாடு, திருநாடு) may be regions or epithets of kings; the verse is a figure of crowded homage either way.
2582.event: Subject kings queue with tribute for an audience with Civakan.

2583.reading: As fish leap in the fishers' yards and deer fatten on the hunters' ground, the age turns, becomes like Uttarakuru, banishes killing and miserliness, and goes on under one ruler.
2583.nuance: Uttarakuru is a land of effortless enjoyment in Jain and Buddhist cosmology. The poet sets the king's peace beside it; he does not say that the cosmic age itself has changed.

claims.claim: a king's rule that ends killing and miserliness makes his land a golden age like Uttarakuru

2584.reading: The poet says he will tell what the doll-like dancer Anangamalai brought about, whose hair lies on her hip like the gold fillet bound on a rutting elephant's brow and who watches for the moments of love.
2584.nuance: This is the poet's turn from praise of the reign to the dancer's story, in the first person (உற்றேன்).

2585.reading: Civakan, whose gold anklets are rubbed by the diamonds of kings' crowns, calls to the lotus-faced young woman who said she would reach her lord's feet and now stands at the outer gate, to come quickly.
2585.nuance: The verse never names the woman; she is Anangamalai because the letter that follows is hers (2586-2590) and 2584 has just announced her.
2585.event: Civakan has Anangamalai, waiting at the gate, called in.

2586.reading: Anangamalai, ashamed like a swan, slips in, bows at the king's feet, folds her slender hands and hands over a letter in the proper manner; he takes it and reads.
2586.event: Anangamalai presents Civakan with a written letter and he reads it.

2587.reading: The letter asks the lord to see it and be pleased, and recalls that, after she had once bowed to him and the cruel spearman in rage had thrown her out of the stage and put her under guard in the temple, she, a girl bound to Kantukkatan, is asked to be granted a favour.
2587.nuance: Lines 3-4 are not fully construable: whether கந்து கற்கு (Kantukkatan's) is the girl's foster-bond, and what is asked, remain unsettled. Line 2 is read as the usurper's anger after her glance at Civakan (685).
2587.event: Anangamalai's letter recalls her bowing to Civakan and the usurper's punishment of her.

2588.reading: The letter goes on that, released because he could no longer bear her crying, she kept to a thatched hut among crowing birds, painted Civakan's image, garlanded and worshipped it; and it asks the king of kings whether he will hide women's love.
2588.nuance: The letter is her own account; the poem has shown her devotion only through her letter. The verse's last clause is a plea, not a proven wrong.
2588.event: Anangamalai writes that she worshipped a painted image of Civakan and asks him not to ignore her.

claims.claim: a woman's love, once openly given, should not be left unanswered by the king

2589.reading: She asks whether the world is to be told that the king lacks friendship, whether women are to give up their lives, and whether those who reach the friendship of the great go away.
2589.nuance: The first three lines describe her wasting: sleepless eyes, loosened bangles and anklets, lost sheen of the body. They are the cost she lays before him, not a narrative.

claims.claim: those who have gained a great one's friendship do not abandon it

2590.reading: Standing under the umbrella that gives the world the shade of dharma, she asks whether she is outside it, and begs the king of kings to grant release now, so that the standing of her friend Vamalekai, who came with her, may not be ruined.
2590.nuance: The claim is her appeal, not the narrator's. What is to be released, and why Vamalekai is named, is unclear: the verse says only that the friend's standing depends on it.
2590.event: Anangamalai petitions Civakan under the figure of his umbrella.

claims.claim: a king's white umbrella is the shade of dharma that shelters the world

2591.reading: On a gold bed made by a skilled craftsman while birds, lute and flute sound, Civakan holds the flower-creeper whose sweet words take the lute's voice, his shoulders swelling and his ear-ornament swinging.
2591.nuance: The woman is not named; she is Anangamalai from the sequence of the letter.
2591.event: Civakan embraces Anangamalai on the royal bed.

2592.reading: Women bring sandal ground on coral stones, flower garlands, thick scented smoke and five-fold perfumes to the garland-chested king and to the woman.
2592.nuance: The attendants and the couple are known only from the context.
2592.event: Attendants bring Civakan and Anangamalai perfumes, sandal and garlands.

2593.reading: Civakan says to Anangamalai that in the delight of wealth he said confused words that measured her mind, and asks how he could forget her; the woman with rolling pearl breasts shows her joy.
2593.nuance: The verse is hard to divide: the question in line 1 and the confession of lines 2-3 are read as the king's, but the speaker is not named.
2593.event: Civakan assures Anangamalai that he has not forgotten her, and she rejoices.

2594.reading: With her moon-like smile, her bent brows, her darting long eyes, and the sounds of her anklets and girdle in time with the music, the dancer plays before the king, who watches the play, his garland opening and her charm melting.
2594.nuance: The king's name வேந்தன் is split across lines 3 and 4, so the agent is tagged by the verb கண்டான்.
2594.event: Anangamalai dances before Civakan, who watches.

2595.reading: Like a four-tusked rutting elephant playing with a lotus-lady, Civakan takes the beauty of the Fortune-like woman while the spear-eyed women praise, and so goes on, the lord of jewels without equal in heaven or on earth.
2595.event: Civakan lives in pleasure with Anangamalai, praised by the women.

2596.reading: To the sound of the lute, drum and flute, the foreign dancing-doll, her wide eyes and red mouth bright, dances on the stage and pleases the king.
2596.nuance: தேசிகப் பாவை, 'the doll of the regional style', is the poet's name for her dancing; the verse does not say she came from elsewhere.

2597.reading: After lovingly releasing the sea-army kings, Civakan drinks the woman like nectar, she who is like a gold shoot on the arrow-wounded king's chest, and she quivers like a tender shoot that the bee drinks.
2597.nuance: கடற்படை மன்னர் is read as the kings with the 'sea-wide army' who fought for him in the last war.
2597.event: Civakan sends the allied kings home and takes Anangamalai to bed.

2598.reading: She, the field of youth ploughed and fenced with gold, her soft shoulders the ridges, bears the seed of beauty; the lord of the lute dwells enjoying the sweet harvest that love ripened from the music and dance.
2598.nuance: The field figure turns the woman's body into land worked and harvested; the verse presents it as praise and does not weigh the cost, a point where the Siddhar texts differ.
2598.event: Civakan enjoys the fruit of love with Anangamalai.

links.note: In 683 the dancer wrote a letter in figure, calling her streaked eyes the letter and her smile the friend who carried it; in 2586 she hands over a letter in the proper manner and he reads it.
links.teaches: The earlier letter of eyes only hinted; the written letter now makes the same appeal in words, which shows the epic turning a figure into a document, so her love must now be answered in the open.

links.note: In 686 the usurper closes on the garlanded dancer and strips her; in 2587 she recounts that, once she had bowed to Civakan, the cruel spearman threw her off the stage and jailed her.
links.teaches: The letter gives the dancer's own account of what 686 told from outside, which shows the violence as something she carries as an injury against Civakan, not only as the usurper's crime.

links.note: In 687 the captive cried out unceasingly to Civakan, the bowman who took her maidenhood; in 2593 the king, now secure, answers 'how could I forget you?'.
links.teaches: The cry in the usurper's grip is answered only after the usurper's fall and a letter, so the epic shows that the king's help comes late, long after her call.

links.note: In 676 her eyes and brows moved as she danced and the watchers were overcome; in 2594 the same eyes and brows play while the king himself watches, his garland opening.
links.teaches: The dance that once undid a crowd of strangers now undoes the one man it was aimed at, which shows how the same art, once open to all, has been turned to a single patron.

links.note: In 684 the dancer rejoiced that his hand had touched her hip and that the toil of bearing young breasts was over; in 2598 the ripened love is enjoyed as a harvest.
links.teaches: The joy in 684 was only a promise made on being touched; 2598 shows what became of it, which is the epic's picture of love as a field worked for a harvest.

links.note: Tirumanthiram 207 says that union with young women is sweet cane juice in the hand and turns bitter neem in the body; 2598 sets the same pleasure as a sweet harvest of love enjoyed in peace.
links.teaches: Set against the Saiva warning, the epic's closing image of the king resting in love reads as a stage in a life the epic itself will end in renunciation, not a conclusion.

gains.a: a counterweight inside the poem's praise of enjoyment, to set against the epic's later turn to the Jina's path
gains.b: a worked scene of the pleasure it warns against, drawn at its sweetest, which shows why the warning is needed

links.note: Anangamalai pleads that she not be left outside the shade of Civakan's white umbrella, which she calls the shade of dharma; Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade but to shelter suffering subjects who may come to him for justice.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem tells a king to keep his umbrella for the sufferer, and the epic shows a sufferer actually using it, which puts the claim to the test of whether a king's sheltering reaches a woman's private petition.

gains.a: an older standard of the umbrella as the king's duty to the suffering, which her petition invokes but the epic does not itself state
gains.b: a petitioner who stands in the position it only imagines, which shows what it asks of a king in practice

links.note: Kural 545 says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who wields the sceptre by its nature; 2583 says that under Civakan killing and miserliness are banished and the land becomes like Uttarakuru, with fish leaping into the fishers' yards.
links.teaches: The couplet's rule is carried to its extreme here, where just rule ends killing and scarcity as well as drought, but the epic offers it only as praise, so the couplet's causal claim remains unproved.

gains.a: the Kural's measure by which the praise is read, rain and harvest as the sign of a just sceptre
gains.b: a case where the sign is raised from rain to a golden age, which shows the couplet's limit: it names the sign but not how far a king's rule can reach

links.note: Naladiyar 371 says the friendship of harlots ends when the hand is empty, as the lamp's light ends when the oil runs out; in 2588 Anangamalai, a woman of the stage, is jailed and released and keeps worshipping a painted image of Civakan with no payment.
links.teaches: The quatrain's rule is a claim about women of her station, and her story tests it, which shows the epic treating constancy as the person's, not the profession's.

gains.a: a hostile frame that makes her constancy a deliberate answer to a standing charge against dancers
gains.b: a counter-case in which a woman of the stage keeps love without income, which shows the rule as a generalisation about types, not a law

source_issues: 2582-2583 and 2584-2598 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2587 lines 3-4 (கந்து கற்குச் சிறுவயானிப் படிய னல்காய்) are hard to construe, and 2590 line 3 (வந்தவென் றோழி வாமலேகை) leaves the reason for the friend's naming unclear.
2593 line 2 (தெருளலான்) and 2594 line 4 (அறியுநாடகங் கண்டான்) are doubtful in sense, and 2594 line 2 (நெறியின்வட்டித்து) is obscure.
2582 line 1 (செருநாடு ... திருநாடு) reads as names or epithets of lands; the sense is not fixed.
